Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

lande (development version)

  • On a server, the app limits a run to 10 traits, 5000 individuals and 20 groups, and draws fewer bootstrap resamples for a large fit, so one Run can’t hold up everyone else. run_app() has no limits.
  • plot_correlated_fitness_3d() draws the fitted fitness surface in 3D as a mesh of grid squares outlined in dark grey, only where there are data, with its interior peaks marked and light shading that shade sets. color_palette = "jet" gives the rainbow ramp of many published surfaces; viridis stays the default as it reads better for colour-blind viewers. The app’s fitness surface tab can show it too, with the group means and high points, and a jet colour theme for the 2D and 3D views.
  • The app is much faster. Run shows the gradients at once, each fit is kept so a change refits only what it affects, and the spline band runs on worker processes (options(lande.workers = 0) turns them off). The landscape now starts on the lattice method.
  • univariate_spline() gains cl to run the bootstrap refits on a cluster, with the same results.
  • bootstrap_selection() refits only the least-squares gradients on each resample and runs 40 to 55 times faster. A resample is no longer dropped when its p-value model would fail to fit.
  • selection_coefficients() no longer fails when a least-squares fit is exact.
  • adaptive_landscape() gains method = "lattice", the same draws as before but 4 to 10 times faster, and method = "convolve", a Gaussian convolution with no simulation noise. The default is unchanged.
  • The app reads semicolon, tab and UTF-16 CSV files and Excel’s Windows encoding, and says why a file can’t be read.
  • The app can download the whole analysis as one zip, with the data and an R script that reruns it.
  • The app has a new layout built around its results, each with its own downloads.

lande 0.1.1

  • adaptive_landscape() holds a numeric group, such as year, at the same reference level as correlated_fitness_surface(). It took the median level of the raw column, while the surface took the most common level, so a landscape from a surface with group = "year" could be drawn at a different year from the surface.
  • The app no longer needs plotly to start: without it, the 3D landscape falls back to the fields plot as intended.
  • The finch_community help page cites the authors’ CC BY 4.0 data deposit on Borealis as its source.
  • The title is now “Standardised Analyses of Natural Selection Data”.
  • The minimum versions of dplyr (1.1.0) and testthat (3.1.7) are set.
  • Smaller fixes to the help pages, the examples and the vignette.

lande 0.1.0

CRAN release: 2026-10-16

First release.

  • Selection differentials and linear, quadratic and correlational gradients on relative fitness, with p-values from the logistic model for survival and from a Poisson or negative binomial model for counts.
  • Cubic spline fitness functions with a bootstrap band, two-trait fitness surfaces drawn only where there are data, and adaptive landscapes of mean fitness for one or two traits.
  • count_family = "quasipoisson" or "nb" in univariate_spline(), correlated_fitness_surface() and temporal_landscape() for overdispersed counts; the spline and the surface report the dispersion.
  • by_group = TRUE in the spline and the surface fits each group on its own and returns a list of fits.
  • Several groups on one surface, with each group’s mean and highest point marked, and interior peaks told from maxima at the edge of the data.
  • Fitness functions and landscapes fitted period by period.
  • Bootstrap standard errors and percentile intervals for the gradients, and leave-one-out (HC3) standard errors with se_type = "hc3".
  • Assumption checks in one table: multivariate normality of the traits, VIF, rows per term, residuals or dispersion of the gradient model.
  • Bumpus’s sparrows, Martin’s pupfish and two sets of Galapagos finches bundled as datasets, with CSV copies of the pupfish and finch data in extdata.
  • A Shiny app that runs the analyses in a browser, opened with run_app(), which writes out the R calls that repeat an analysis with the current settings.
  • canonical_analysis() rotates the gamma matrix to its canonical axes, with double-regression standard errors, permutation p-values (Reynolds et al.
    1. and an optional bootstrap, and plot_canonical_axes() draws fitness along them.
  • Standard errors and a band on the GAM fitness surface, drawn with the plots’ uncertainty option, and peak_difference() to compare two points of a surface, or each with the pass between them (route = "line" for the straight line).
  • The adaptive landscape reports how much of each simulated population falls outside the data, and flags an optimum on the edge of the grid; the plot can mark where the population leaves the data.
  • A clamp option on the landscape and the thin-plate surface holds predicted fitness inside the range of the fitness type; on by default.
